text: Drag Force and Terminal Speed You feel the drag force when you move your hand through water or during a strong wind, EG outside the car window. The faster you move your hand, the harder it is to move. You feel a smaller drag force when you tilt your hand so only the side goes through the air, EG decreased your surface area in the direction of motion. Drag Forces The drag force always opposes the motion of an object like friction. Unlike simple friction, the drag force is proportional to some function of the velocity of the object in that fluid. Which function to choose is complicated and depends on several factors, shape of the object, its aerodynamics, size, velocity, and the fluid it is in. For most large objects, EG cyclists, cars, baseballs, not moving too slowly, the magnitude of the drag force F sub D is proportional to the square of the speed of the object. EG F sub D is proportional to V squared. The full relationship becomes vector F sub D equals 1 half C rho A V squared V hat, where C is the drag coefficient, A is the cross-sectional area, EG side facing the fluid, and rho is the density of the fluid. Recall that density is mass per unit volume, rho equals M over V. The more generalized form is F sub D equals B to the power of N, where the constant B equals 0.5 C rho A bundles all the constants together. The exponent N equals 2 comes from our assumption about moving at high speed. If the object is moving a low speed, then N equals 1. Checkpoint. Pause and check your understanding. If the speed doubles in the quadratic drag model, by what factor does the drag force change? Athletes as well as car designers seek to reduce the drag force to lower their race times. Aerodynamic shaping of an automobile can reduce the drag force, and thus increase the car's gas mileage. The value of the drag coefficient is determined empirically, either by using a wind tunnel, or through a complex numerical simulation on a supercomputer. The drag coefficient can depend on velocity, but we assume that it is constant here. See the table, typical values of drag coefficient, below that lists some typical drag coefficients for a variety of objects, while drag coefficients by geometric shape provides values by the geometric shape. The drag coefficient is a dimensionless quantity. The course webpage includes tables of typical drag coefficients. At highway speeds, over 50% of the power of the car is used to overcome air drag. For average conditions, for example altitude and temperature, the most fuel-efficient cruising speed is about 45 to 50 mph, or about 70 to 80 kmh. Substantial research is undertaken to minimize drag in racing sports, as well as specific sporting instruments. For example, the dimples on golf balls are being redesigned, as well as the clothes athletes wear. Most elite swimmers and cyclists shave their body hair to reduce drag and can slice milliseconds off a race time, which can be the difference between a gold or silver medal. Terminal velocity. Consider a skydiver falling under the influence of gravity. The two forces acting on him are the force of gravity, F sub G, and the drag force, F sub D. Ignoring the small buoyant force caused by displacing the air. The downward force of gravity remains roughly constant, i.e., the altitude above Earth's surface is much less than Earth's radius, and does not depend on his velocity. However, the magnitude of the drag force increases with velocity squared, assuming his descent is sufficiently fast, until it equals the gravitational force, thus producing a net force of zero and stops accelerating. At this point, the person's velocity remains constant, and he has reached his terminal velocity, V sub T. At the terminal velocity, F net equals F sub D minus F sub G equals MA equals zero. F sub D equals F sub G equals MG. Using equation, we solve for V sub T, one over two, C row A, V sub T to the power of two equals MG. V sub T to the power of two equals 2 MG over row CA. V sub T equals square root of 2 MG over row CA. Checkpoint. Pause and check your understanding. At terminal velocity, are the forces gone, or are the upward and downward forces balanced? Assume the density of air is row equals 1.21 kilograms per cubic meter, and a skydiver with a mass of 75 kilograms, whose cross-sectional area is A equals 0.18 square meters. He has a drag coefficient, C equals 0.70, which means we can calculate his terminal velocity, V sub T as... V sub T equals square root of two times 75 kilograms times 9.81 meters per second squared over 1.21 kilograms per cubic meter times 0.70 times 0.18 square meters equals 98 meters per second equals 350 kilometers per hour. This means a skydiver with a mass of 75 kilograms achieves a terminal velocity of 350 kilometers per hour in a head first position, minimizing the area and his drag, 200 kilometers per hour in a spread-ego position, area has increased. Equation does not hold if the object is very small, is going very slow, or is in a denser medium than air. For these cases, we find the drag force is proportional to just the velocity, that is, F sub D is proportional to V. This relation is given by Stokes law. Stokes law. For a spherical object falling in a medium, the drag force is VF sub S equals 6 pi R eta Vector V, where R is the radius of the sphere, eta is the viscosity of the fluid, and Vector V is the object's velocity. Good examples of Stokes law are provided by microorganisms, pollen, and dust particles. Each of these objects is small, where we find that many of these objects travel unated only at a constant terminal velocity. Example problem. Terminal velocity of a skydiver. The problem. Find the terminal velocity of an 85 kilograms skydiver falling in a spread-ego position. Assume that in the spread-ego position, the diver has a cross-sectional area of 0.70 square meters. The worked solution follows. The model. The skydiver is modeled as a particle falling vertically through air. We choose plus j-hat upward, so the drag force points in the plus j-hat direction during the downward fall, and the weight points in the negative j-hat direction. At terminal velocity, the skydiver moves at constant speed, so the acceleration is 0. The drag force is modeled with the quadratic drag law. Air density and drag coefficient are treated as constant. The math. At terminal velocity, the skydiver requires zero net force, because the acceleration is 0. The forces acting on the skydiver are the upward drag force and the downward weight. We substitute the drag expression into the terminal velocity force balance and solve for v sub t. 1 over 2 rho ca v sub t to the power of 2 equals mg. v sub t to the power of 2 equals 2 mg over rho ca. For a spread-eagle skydiver, we use c equals 1.0 and rho equals 1.21 kilograms per cubic meter. The terminal speed follows from the drag weight balance using c equals 1.0, rho equals 1.21 kilograms per cubic meter and the given cross-sectional area. v sub t equals square root of 2 times 85 kilograms times 9.81 meters per second squared, over 1.21 kilograms per cubic meter times 1.0 times 0.70 square meters equals 44 meters per second. The conclusion. The terminal velocity of the skydiver in a spread-eagle position is 44 meters per second downward. At this speed, the upward drag force balances the skydiver's weight, so the acceleration is 0 and the speed remains constant. The calculus of velocity-dependent frictional forces. However, for a body moving in a straight line at moderate speeds through a liquid such as water, frictional force can be approximated by f sub r equals negative b times v, where b is a constant whose value depends on the dimensions and shape of the body and the properties of the liquid. Consider an object falling through a liquid. Newton's second law in the vertical direction gives the differential equation, mg minus bv equals m times dv over dt, where we have written the acceleration as dv over dt. As v increases, the frictional force increases until it matches the weight mg. At this point, there is no acceleration and the velocity remains constant at the terminal velocity v sub t. Thus, we have mg minus b times v sub t equals 0 and v sub t equals mg divided by b. Checkpoint. Pause and check your understanding. And negative m over b times the natural log of g minus b over m times v prime evaluated from 0 to v equals t prime evaluated from 0 to t, where v prime and t prime are dummy variables of integration. Applying the limits of integration, we find negative m over b times the quantity natural log of g minus b over m times v minus natural log of g equals t. Natural log of a divided by b equals x, then e to the x equals a divided by b. Using the properties of logarithms, we find a divided by b equals the quantity g minus b v over m divided by g, which equals e to the power of b t over m. Solving for v, we find v equals m over b times the quantity 1 minus e to the negative b t over m. v equals m g over b times the quantity 1 minus e to the power of b t over m. Notice that as t approaches infinity, v approaches m g over b, which equals v sub t, the terminal velocity. The position at any time can be found by integrating the equation for v. B, if the boat slows down from 4.0 meters per second to 1.0 meters per second in 10 seconds, how far does it travel before stopping? The worked solution follows. The model. The motorboat is modeled as a particle moving horizontally across the lake. We choose plus i hat to point in the initial direction of motion. After the motor stops, the only horizontal force is the resistive force vector f sub r equals minus b v i hat, which points opposite the velocity. Vertical forces balance and do not affect the horizontal motion. The resistive force is proportional to speed, so the acceleration changes as the boat slows. The math. As t becomes very large, the exponential term approaches zero, so the limiting distance is x sub max equals m v sub zero over b. Next, we use the observed slowing of the boat to determine b over m. The velocity function gives v over v sub zero equals e to the power of negative b t over m. The observed decrease in speed determines the ratio b over m, 1.0 meters per second over 4.0 meters per second equals e to the power of negative b over m times 10 seconds. 0.25 equals e to the power of negative 10 b over m. We take the natural logarithm and solve for b over m. Natural log of 0.25 equals negative 10 b over m. b over m equals natural log of 4.0 over 10 seconds equals 0.14 seconds to the power of negative 1. The stopping distance is the limiting distance from part a. The boat's velocity decreases exponentially according to v of t equals v sub zero e to the power of negative b t over m. And its position is x of t equals m v sub zero over b times 1 minus e to the power of negative b t over m. The boat approaches a limiting distance x sub max equals m v sub zero over b. For the given slowing data, the boat travels approximately 29 meters before effectively stopping.
